# Muni Sutta (Snp 1.12 (PTS Snp 35))

**ID:** Snp 1.12 (PTS Snp 35)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Muni Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Munisutta* ("The Sage", Snp 1.12) is the twelfth discourse of the Uragavagga in the *Suttanipāta* [Hazra 1994]. The poem describes the attributes of the ideal sage (*muni*), celebrating the solitary, wandering forest ascetic who finds peace and security far from domestic ties, overcomes spiritual obstacles, and has transcended speculative sophistry (*takka*) [Boucher 2008; Webster 2005]. Rhetorically, nine verses in the discourse conclude with the recurring refrain *taṃ vā pi dhīrā muniṃ vedayanti* ("him the wise declare to be a sage") [Katre 1931]. A well-known stanza contrasts the solitary forest mendicant with the householder using the simile of a wild goose or swan whose flight cannot be matched by a peacock [Lamotte 1988; Thich Thien Chau 1996]. The commentary (*Paramatthajotikā*) regards the sutta as an anthology of originally independent verses uttered by the Buddha on different occasions [Lamotte 1988].

Scholars generally identify the sutta with the *Munigāthā* mentioned in King Aśoka's Bhairat (Bhabru) edict among the texts recommended for reflection [Thomas 1933; Winternitz 1933; Wynne 2007]. Outside the Pali canon, Northern Buddhist literature such as the *Divyāvadāna* mentions the recitation of the *Munigāthā* alongside the *Śailagāthā* and the *Arthavargīya* [Hazra 1994], and the title is attested in Chinese transcriptions (*Mou-ni-chieh*) [Dhammapala et al. 1984]. In later Pali literature, the sutta is quoted in the *Milindapañha* (*Santhavapañha*, Mil 5.5.1, and *Vāyuṅgapañha*, Mil 7.4.4).

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Mentioned in: Mil 5.5.1 Santhavapañha; Mil 7.4.4 Vāyuṅgapañha

**Sources**

- [Boucher 2008] Daniel Boucher, Bodhisattvas of the Forest and the Formation of the Mahāyāna: The Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra (2008) — Notes the sutta's theme of the forest sage and its association with King Aśoka.
- [Dhammapala et al. 1984] Gatare Dhammapala, Richard Gombrich, and K. R. Norman (eds.), Buddhist Studies in Honour of Hammalava Saddhatissa (1984) — Identifies the Chinese title Mou-ni-chieh as corresponding to the Munigāthā / Munisutta.
- [Katre 1931] S. M. Katre, Early Buddhist Ballads and Their Relation to Older Upanishadic Literature (1931) — Identifies the refrain recurring nine times in the sutta.
- [Thomas 1933] Edward J. Thomas, History of Buddhist Thought (1933) — Connects the Munigāthā of the Aśokan edicts to the Munisutta (Sn 1.12).
- [Lamotte 1988] Étienne Lamotte, History of Indian Buddhism (1988 [1958]) — Discusses the peacock/swan simile and the commentary's view of the sutta as an artificial collection of verses.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Identifies the Aśokan title Munigāthā with the Munisutta.
- [Nakamura 1980] Hajime Nakamura, Indian Buddhism: A Survey with Bibliographical Notes (1980) — Notes scholarship comparing the Munisutta with passages in the Mahāvastu.
- [Thich Thien Chau 1996] Thich Thien Chau, The Literature of the Personalists of Early Buddhism (1996) — Quotes and discusses the peacock and wild goose simile in the Munisutta.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Discusses the mention of Munigāthā in the Divyāvadāna and its place in the Uragavagga.
- [Webster 2005] David Webster, The Philosophy of Desire in the Buddhist Pali Canon (2005) — Discusses overcoming takka (sophistry/reasoning) in the Muni Sutta.
- [Wynne 2007] Alexander Wynne, The Origin of Buddhist Meditation (2007) — Discusses Aśoka's Bhairat edict, the verse range (Sn 207–221), and Mahāvastu parallels.
